parole.significato: To dismiss (someone, especially military personnel) from service.
parole.testo: From Dutch casseren, kasseren, from Old French casser (“to break (up)”). During a ceremonial cashiering of a ranking military officer, the breakup was often symbolized dramatically by literally breaking the officer’s sword.
An alteration of Dutch genever under the influence of the geonym Geneva.

parole.significato: A colourless non-aged alcoholic liquor made by distilling fermented grains such as barley, corn, oats or rye with junip…
parole.testo: Abbreviation of geneva, alteration of Dutch genever (“juniper”) from Old French genevre (modern French genièvre), from Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus (“juniper”). Hence gin rummy (first attested 1941).

parole.significato: A Dutch and Flemish alcoholic spirit, flavoured with juniper, rather like gin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch jenever (“jenever”), from Old French genevre, from Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus (“juniper”).

parole.significato: A kind of large cupboard or wardrobe of Dutch origin, popular in the Netherlands and America in the 17th and 18th centu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch kas (“cupboard, chest, case”), from Middle Dutch kasse, casse, from Old French casse, from Latin capsa (“box, chest, case”).

parole.significato: A tract of soft, wet ground; a marsh; a fen.
parole.testo: From Dutch moeras (“marsh, swamp”), an alteration (with influence from Dutch moer (“moor”)) of a direct descendant of Middle Dutch marasch (“marsh”). The Middle Dutch word is a borrowing from Old French mareis, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk. Doublet of marish and marsh, and linked in part to moor
From Dutch ruiter, from Middle Dutch ruter, from Old French routier.
First attested in 1687. Origin uncertain, but possibly from Dutch schamperen, from Old French escamper, from Vulgar Latin *excampāre.
From earlier Dutch succoreye, sukereye (Modern Dutch suikerij (“chicory”)), from Middle Dutch, from Old French cicorée. Doublet of chicory.
